items.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006
items.q: Carla Bley and Mike Mantler were doing things and they invited me to do tuba on some of their things. I actually sang on one of their — “Escalator Over the Hill,” that, one of those early JCOA albums. And then I played on some of her other things and that’s when I was in her band

ctx.x: Did you find that okay you’re playing an instrument that not as many people play perhaps, especially in the jazz world, so there’s not as much competition on your instrument but there’s not as many opportunities? Or did you make your opportunities?

I think both things are probably true. And to one degree or another both things are true at whatever given time. When I first came to New York the only opportunity for tuba was at Your Father’s Moustache, and soon after that, around ’67, McCoy Tyner had recorded an album called “Tender Moments,” all right? With Lee Morgan and James Spaulding, and just some great players. And he was doing some work with that album in New York at Slugs, it was before McCoy was of the stature to be able to go into the Vanguard and…

with being an ensemble horn player in these big band settings. So there were two different positions that I got a chance to be in. And also because of the many hats that I’ve worn I was playing free jazz in Sam Rivers’ Big Band that was performing and working and rehearsing at this time all through the seventies, I was playing Collective Black Artists Big Winds, which was a kind of a cultural, very ethnic — it was swing and everything but it still had a more cultural and ethnic quality to it. Then I was also…

items.title: Bley Carla — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Michael Mantler. Bob Stewart. ... Vincent Chancey, he was even in my band ... Bob, no. John Clark, French Horn. ... [INTERVIEWER] ... was Bob Stewart on the tuba. [INTERVIEWEE] Oh!

ctx.x: So who in those early days in the band, some of those players in the band that you can recall?

Michael Mantler. Bob Stewart. Or Joe Daley. Either one of those two guys. Vincent Chancey, he was even in my band when we sang. We had a singing band for a while. We all sang. Oh! That’s the album I Hate To Sing. No it isn’t... Yeah it is. But I had all the guys sing. Joe Daley would be singing! It was amazing what they did, what

we did. But I’m trying to remember the guys in the band. They were also in more serious bands. George Lewis, the smart trombone player from MIT. “Blue” Gene Tyranny from the classical world, piano player. Don Preston sometimes was the organ player or the synthesizer player. Bob, no. John Clark, French Horn. Gary Windo, tenor. Allan Braufman, alto. Sometimes Joe Lovano, tenor. Eventually Steve Slagle, alto. These are names I remember, I saw these guys hundreds of times, and wrote for them.
